newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb opposition drops protests - for time being.
newsitem.headline: Serb opposition drops protests - for time being.

text.p: Serbia's opposition said it would give the authorities a three-week breather after three months of continual street protests but it coupled the concession with an ultimatum.

"Let us give them a chance to show an intention to free the media and, if they fail to do that by March 9, then what else can we do but go out into the streets again," said Zoran Djindjic, co-leader of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition.

He was addressing around 10,000 people in central Belgrade -- a fraction of the 500,000 that took to the streets at the height of the protests -- on the 88th straight day of anti-government demonstrations.
Djindjic said the opposition had achieved one of its main aims, the recognition of opposition gains in local elections last November, but still had two key goals.

"Our three objectives were to get back our election victory and achieve the deblocking of the media and fair conditions ahead of the next elections. We have achieved the first, but not the other two," he said.

With parliamentary and presidential elections scheduled for later this year, the role of the broadcasting media, which is firmly under the control of authoritarian President Slobodan Milosevic, has emerged as a key issue.

Independent Belgrade radio stations gave full coverage of Saturday's opposition rally but they can barely be heard outside the capital. The majority of the population in small towns and villages haa to rely on state TV and radio.
Zajedno launched its protest campaign after the government, citing unspecified voting irregularities, annulled its victories in 14 towns and cities including Belgrade in the local elections.
The government finally caved in to pressure from the streets and from abroad and introduced a special law recognising the election results.

But the opposition has made clear that it is looking beyond the local polls to the general elections and wants a major reform of Serbia's centralised system which has been in place largely unchanged for five decades.
"All our institutions are only an instrument for preserving the regime and that is why we must persevere in the struggle to achieve our aims," Djindjic told the crowd.

"Serbia is like a man half-way down in quicksand. He cannot stay there for ever, he must either get out or sink and die. We must continue our struggle in order to protect the elementary right we have won, the right to our dignity."
Another of the three opposition leaders, Vuk Draskovic, described that victory over the local election results as "only the first step, but an enormous step."
"We cannot change the passengers in our bus, but we must change the driver," he told the crowd.
Opposition leaders said they would hold a celebration party on Friday to mark the first session of the opposition-led local council in Belgrade.
"Prepare well, because it will be jolly and it could last all night," said opposition co-leader Vesna Pesic.

Belgrade students who have also held daily protests said they would continue their demonstrations until the government sacked the university rector and prosecuted those responsible for annulling the local election results.
